patient.name: Priya Sharma
patient.setting: GP surgery, then maternity assessment unit
patient.complaint: Burning on passing urine and going every hour for 2 days
background: 31 weeks pregnant with her first baby
Two UTIs in the past year, both after intercourse

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a lower versus upper UTI decision (fever, loin pain), or the causative organism, usually E. coli.

points: Priya, 29, **31 weeks pregnant** with her first baby.
Going every hour; urgent; urine cloudy and smelly.
No fever, no loin pain, no vaginal discharge.

steps.lead: Dysuria and frequency in a young woman: an infection of the lower urinary tract, most likely **E. coli**.
Priya is female, sexually active and **pregnant**: three risk factors at once.

visual.title: Where Priya is tender today
visual.caption: Suprapubic tenderness without loin pain: lower UTI (cystitis).

steps.lead: Priya has **lower UTI** symptoms only: dysuria, frequency, urgency and no systemic features.

steps.q: Priya has dysuria, frequency and suprapubic tenderness, with no fever. Which is it?
steps.r: No fever, no loin pain: **cystitis**. Fever, rigors and flank pain would make it pyelonephritis.

steps.lead: Priya now has the signature of **acute pyelonephritis**: fever, rigors, loin pain, renal angle tenderness and vomiting.
Priya's rising heart rate and falling BP are warning signs: pyelonephritis can progress to **sepsis**.
Flank discomfort in someone with type 2 diabetes means **complicated** UTI. Sterile cystitis in a ketamine user is ketamine cystitis.

steps.text: Fever + loin pain + renal angle tenderness = **upper** UTI. No systemic features = **lower** UTI.

investigation.exam: Expect dipstick versus MSU culture (age over 65), culture as the gold standard and test of cure in pregnancy.

steps.q: Priya is under 65. What is the first test at the bedside?
steps.r: A **dipstick** for leucocytes and nitrites first; culture follows because she is pregnant.

steps.title: Priya's urine dipstick
steps.text: Leucocytes and nitrites together strongly suggest infection.

steps.lead: Priya's dipstick is helpful. If she were **over 65**, a dipstick would not be enough: send an MSU for microscopy and culture.
Priya is **pregnant**, so she needs a **urine culture**, the gold standard, to guide antibiotics.

steps.title: Priya's MSU culture
steps.text: Sensitivities steer the choice, especially when pregnancy rules drugs out.

steps.lead: After treatment Priya sends a **test-of-cure MSU** to prove the infection has gone.

steps.title: Which urine test, for whom?
nodes: Over 65, or women with haematuria: MSU culture
Pregnant: culture, then test of cure
Men and pyelonephritis: culture to guide antibiotics

steps.text: A positive dipstick in someone **over 65** is unreliable. Send an MSU for culture.

management.exam: Expect the antibiotic and duration by group: women, men, pregnancy trimester, catheters, pyelonephritis.

visual.title: Pregnancy and UTI antibiotics
visual.label: Priya 31 weeks
visual.caption: Trimethoprim risks neural tube defects early; nitrofurantoin risks neonatal haemolysis late.

steps.q: Before her fever, which antibiotic suits Priya's cystitis at 31 weeks?
steps.r: In the **third trimester** avoid nitrofurantoin; **cefalexin or amoxicillin** if sensitivities support.

steps.lead: If Priya were not pregnant, **nitrofurantoin for 3 days** would be first-line. Know each drug's pitfalls.

steps.title: Nitrofurantoin vs trimethoprim
head: Issue
Nitrofurantoin
Trimethoprim
rows: Preferred in CKD; isolated creatinine rise

steps.lead: Priya is pregnant, so **cefalexin** in the third trimester. Men always get 7 days; catheter bacteriuria without symptoms is not treated.
If first-line fails in a non-pregnant woman, **pivmecillinam** is the second-line option.

steps.q: Priya now has pyelonephritis with tachycardia. What does she need?
steps.r: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy means admission and **IV cefuroxime**. Oral cystitis treatment is no longer enough.

steps.lead: Priya is admitted for **IV cefuroxime**, the pregnancy choice for pyelonephritis.

visual.title: Priya on IV cefuroxime
visual.caption: Fever and tachycardia settle over 48 to 72 hours on the right antibiotic.

steps.lead: After the baby, Priya's post-intercourse UTIs could be managed with **post-coital nitrofurantoin**.

steps.text: Durations: **3 days** for uncomplicated women; **7 days** for men, pregnant and immunosuppressed women.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanisms: ascending infection, why nitrites are positive, why pregnancy and catheters change the rules.

steps.lead: Priya's infection **ascended**: bowel E. coli colonised the periurethral area and climbed to her bladder, then kidney.
Priya's **short urethra** close to the anus is why women get far more UTIs than men.
Progesterone **dilated Priya's ureters** and slowed peristalsis, which is why her cystitis climbed to her kidney.

steps.q: Why was Priya's nitrite test positive?
o: Gram-negative bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite
Blood in urine reacts with the strip
The kidney excretes nitrite in infection
steps.r: **E. coli** turns dietary nitrate into nitrite. **Leucocyte esterase** is the marker of white cells.

steps.lead: Nitrites = Gram-negative bacteria; leucocyte esterase = pyuria. Priya had both.
Priya's fever and tachycardia came from **kidney parenchymal infection**, which drives a much bigger cytokine response.
If Priya ever had a catheter, bacteria would form a **biofilm** on it; bacteriuria alone would not need treating.

glossary.Cystitis: Infection or inflammation of the bladder; lower UTI.
glossary.Pyelonephritis: Infection of the kidney; upper UTI.
glossary.Dysuria: Pain or burning on passing urine.
glossary.Frequency: Passing urine more often than normal.
glossary.Urgency: Sudden strong need to pass urine.
glossary.Suprapubic: Just above the pubic bone, over the bladder.
glossary.Costovertebral angle: Angle between the 12th rib and spine, over the kidney.
glossary.Renal angle: Same as the costovertebral angle; tender in pyelonephritis.
glossary.Rigors: Episodes of violent shivering with fever.
glossary.Uropathogen: An organism that commonly causes urinary infection.
glossary.E. coli: Escherichia coli, a Gram-negative gut bacterium and the commonest cause of UTI.
glossary.Proteus: Gram-negative urease-producing bacterium linked to UTIs and struvite stones.
glossary.Enterococcus: Gram-positive gut bacterium; less common cause of UTI.
glossary.Emphysematous pyelonephritis: Necrotising kidney infection with gas in the tissue, mainly in diabetics.
glossary.Ketamine cystitis: Bladder damage from chronic ketamine use: thick wall, small contracted bladder.
glossary.Complicated UTI: UTI in men, pregnancy, abnormal urinary tract, catheters or systemic illness.
glossary.Asymptomatic bacteriuria: Bacteria in the urine without symptoms.
glossary.Leucocyte esterase: Enzyme from white cells detected on a dipstick; marker of pyuria.
glossary.Nitrites: Made when Gram-negative bacteria convert nitrate; positive dipstick suggests infection.
glossary.MSU: Midstream urine sample, sent for microscopy and culture.
glossary.Urine culture: Growing bacteria from urine to identify them and their antibiotic sensitivities.
glossary.Test-of-cure: Repeat culture after treatment to confirm the infection has gone.
glossary.Nitrofurantoin: First-line antibiotic for uncomplicated lower UTI.
glossary.Trimethoprim: Folate antagonist antibiotic for UTI; avoid in first trimester.
glossary.Fosfomycin: Alternative oral antibiotic for uncomplicated lower UTI.
glossary.Pivmecillinam: Penicillin-type antibiotic used second-line for lower UTI.
glossary.Cefalexin: Oral cephalosporin used for UTI in late pregnancy and complicated UTI.
glossary.Cefuroxime: IV cephalosporin used for pyelonephritis in pregnancy.
glossary.Ciprofloxacin: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for severe pyelonephritis.
glossary.Co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid; oral option for non-severe pyelonephritis.
glossary.G6PD deficiency: Inherited enzyme deficiency where some drugs cause haemolysis.
glossary.Neonatal haemolysis: Destruction of the newborn's red cells; risk with late-pregnancy nitrofurantoin.
glossary.Neural tube defects: Birth defects of brain or spine such as spina bifida.
glossary.CrCl: Creatinine clearance, an estimate of kidney function.
glossary.Methotrexate: Folate antagonist; dangerous with trimethoprim (marrow suppression).
glossary.Biofilm: Layer of bacteria stuck to a surface such as a catheter, protected from antibiotics.
glossary.Post-coital prophylaxis: A single antibiotic dose after sex to prevent UTI.
glossary.Peristalsis: Waves of muscle contraction that push urine down the ureter.
glossary.Trimester: One of three roughly 13-week periods of pregnancy.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency and today developed fever, rigors and left loin pain. She has vomited twice. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg. She has left renal angle tenderness. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes 2+ and nitrites positive. Her pregnancy test is negative.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: decide lower vs upper UTI.

clues: fever, rigors and left loin pain
steps.x: Urinary symptoms progressing to systemic features with loin tenderness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Upper UTI: **acute pyelonephritis**.

elim: RIF pain and peritonism, not loin pain with infected urine.
Cystitis has no fever, rigors or loin pain.
Lower abdominal pain, discharge, cervical excitation.
Colicky loin-to-groin pain; no nitrites or fever.

steps.x: **C. Acute pyelonephritis.** UTI + fever + loin pain = pyelonephritis.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman has acute pyelonephritis. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. She is starting empirical antibiotics and the team want to confirm the organism and its sensitivities.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: 'Confirm the organism and sensitivities': the gold standard.

clues: confirm the organism and its sensitivities
steps.x: Pyelonephritis needs culture to guide antibiotics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urine culture**.

elim: Looks for stones or obstruction, not the organism.
Shows obstruction, not the bug.
Shows inflammation only.
Screens; it cannot give sensitivities.

steps.x: **D. Urine culture.** Gold standard for UTI = urine culture.

technique.stem: A 42 year old man has 3 days of dysuria and frequency. He is otherwise well with no loin pain. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Nitrofurantoin for 7 days with urine culture

steps.x: Management of a UTI in a special group: men.
Lower UTI in a man: always complicated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat for **7 days** and send a **urine culture**.

elim: For severe pyelonephritis; he is well.
3 days is for women; men need 7.
Second-line for women, and too short for a man.
Symptomatic UTI in a man needs treatment.

steps.x: **C. Nitrofurantoin for 7 days with urine culture.** UTI in men = complicated: 7 days plus culture.

technique.stem: A 23 year old woman has dysuria and frequency. Urine dipstick shows nitrites positive and leucocytes 2+. Culture later grows Escherichia coli.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the positive nitrite test?
o: Bacterial conversion of dietary nitrate to nitrite
Breakdown of red cells in the urine

steps.x: Science: explain a dipstick finding.
Gram-negative E. coli on culture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gram-negative bacteria **reduce nitrate to nitrite**.

elim: Blood gives a separate blood reading.
That causes the leucocyte reading, not nitrites.
The kidney does not secrete nitrite.
Urease makes ammonia (Proteus), not nitrite.

steps.x: **A. Bacterial conversion of dietary nitrate to nitrite.** Nitrites = Gram-negative bacteria; leucocytes = pyuria.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has 2 days of burning when passing urine, frequency and urgency. She has no vaginal discharge. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She has mild suprapubic tenderness and no loin tenderness. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes 2+ and nitrites positive.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Dysuria, frequency and urgency with suprapubic tenderness and no systemic features is cystitis. Pyelonephritis needs fever and loin pain.

steps.x: Diagnosis: lower or upper UTI.

clues: burning when passing urine, frequency and urgency
suprapubic tenderness and no loin tenderness
steps.x: Urinary symptoms only, no systemic features, positive dipstick.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lower UTI (cystitis)**.

elim: No fever, rigors or loin tenderness.
Colicky loin-to-groin pain, not dysuria.
Usually with discharge and negative nitrites.
Itch and discharge; urine is not infected.

steps.x: **A. Cystitis.** No fever, no loin pain = cystitis.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman has 1 day of fever, rigors and right loin pain after a week of dysuria. She has vomited three times. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. She has right costovertebral angle tenderness. Her pregnancy test is negative.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, rigors, loin pain and renal angle tenderness with infected urine is acute pyelonephritis. Cystitis has no systemic features.

steps.x: Diagnosis: lower or upper UTI.

clues: fever, rigors and right loin pain
steps.x: Systemic features plus loin tenderness after cystitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute pyelonephritis**.

elim: RIF pain without urinary symptoms.
No systemic features in cystitis.
Discharge, cervical excitation, lower pain.
Colicky pain; no fever or pyuria.

steps.x: **D. Pyelonephritis.** Fever + loin pain + renal angle tenderness = pyelonephritis.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman has dysuria and frequency starting 2 days after sexual intercourse. She is otherwise well. Her temperature is 37.0°C. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites positive. A midstream urine sample is sent for culture.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: E. coli from bowel flora causes most UTIs and is nitrite positive. Staph. saprophyticus occurs in young women but is far less common.

steps.x: Causative organism: the most common one wins unless a clue says otherwise.
Simple ascending UTI in a young woman, nitrite positive (Gram-negative).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **E. coli**.

elim: Less common; nitrite negative.
A uropathogen but much less common.
Associated with stones and alkaline urine.
Seen in young women, but E. coli is still the most common.

steps.x: **B. Escherichia coli.** Most common uropathogen = E. coli.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has 3 days of fever, right loin pain and confusion. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. CT shows gas within the right renal parenchyma.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a necrotising infection with gas in the renal parenchyma, typically in diabetics. It needs broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a severe UTI complication.

clues: gas within the right renal parenchyma
steps.x: Diabetic, septic, gas in the kidney.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Emphysematous pyelonephritis**.

elim: A collection around the kidney, not gas in the parenchyma.
Slow onset; not septic.
Nephrotic patients; no gas.
Chronic, with a staghorn stone; not acute gas.

steps.x: **A. Emphysematous pyelonephritis.** Diabetes + gas in renal parenchyma = emphysematous pyelonephritis.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant has a routine antenatal urine culture. She has no urinary symptoms. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. A repeat culture also grows the same organism.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A significant pure growth without symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria. In pregnancy it is treated to prevent pyelonephritis.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a finding on routine screening.

clues: repeat culture also grows the same organism
steps.x: Significant pure growth on two samples without symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Asymptomatic bacteriuria**, which must be treated in pregnancy.

elim: Needs symptoms; she has none.
A repeat sample grows the same pure organism.
No fever or loin pain.
Needs symptoms and is usually sexually transmitted.

steps.x: **B. Asymptomatic bacteriuria.** Bacteria on culture, no symptoms, pregnant = treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has fever, rigors and dysuria. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes 3+ and nitrites positive. She has acute pyelonephritis.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Acute pyelonephritis classically causes costovertebral (renal) angle tenderness. Murphy's and Rovsing's signs belong to the gallbladder and appendix.

steps.x: Most likely examination finding for a named diagnosis.
Pyelonephritis = infection of the kidney.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Renal angle (costovertebral angle) tenderness**.

elim: A sign of PID or ectopic pregnancy.
Cholecystitis.
Appendicitis.
Ascites.

steps.x: **B. Costovertebral angle tenderness.** Pyelonephritis on examination = renal angle tenderness.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman has 3 days of dysuria, frequency and new urgency. She is alert and orientated. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. She has no loin pain.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Dipsticks are not recommended as the sole test in patients over 65, so MSU microscopy and culture is first-line. Blood cultures are for systemic illness.

steps.x: Initial investigation in a special group: age over 65.
Over 65: dipsticks are unreliable (bacteriuria is common).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Send an **MSU for microscopy and culture**.

elim: She is not systemically unwell.
For stones, not uncomplicated UTI.
Not first-line for a UTI.
Not recommended as the sole test over 65.

steps.x: **C. Midstream urine microscopy and culture.** Over 65 = MSU culture, not dipstick alone.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant was treated for a lower UTI with nitrofurantoin. Her symptoms have resolved. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: Pregnant women need a test-of-cure MSU after treatment because untreated bacteriuria can progress to pyelonephritis.

steps.x: 'Next' investigation after treatment in pregnancy.
Pregnant woman after UTI treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **test-of-cure MSU**.

elim: She is well and afebrile.
Pregnant women need proof of eradication.
Not routinely needed after simple cystitis.
Cannot confirm eradication.

steps.x: **E. Test-of-cure MSU.** Pregnant + treated UTI = test-of-cure MSU.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency. She is not pregnant and has normal renal function. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Nitrofurantoin for 3 days is first-line for uncomplicated lower UTI in non-pregnant women. Seven days is for men and pregnant women.

steps.x: Management of uncomplicated lower UTI in a woman.
Uncomplicated cystitis, no contraindications.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Nitrofurantoin for 3 days**.

elim: High resistance and too long.
Reserved for severe pyelonephritis.
7 days is for men and pregnant women.
An alternative, but 3 days, and not first-line.

steps.x: **C. Nitrofurantoin for 3 days.** Uncomplicated woman = nitrofurantoin 3 days.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant has dysuria and frequency. She is afebrile with no loin pain. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. Urine culture sensitivities are below.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
practice.e: In the third trimester nitrofurantoin is avoided because of neonatal haemolysis, so cefalexin is used when sensitive. Trimethoprim is resistant here.

steps.x: Antibiotic choice in a special group: third trimester.
Lower UTI in the third trimester.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cefalexin** (or amoxicillin) if sensitive.

elim: Not used for cystitis in pregnancy.
Contraindicated in pregnancy.
Avoid in the third trimester (neonatal haemolysis).
Resistant on culture.

steps.x: **A. Cefalexin.** Third trimester cystitis = cefalexin or amoxicillin.

practice.stem: An 81 year old man has had a long-term urinary catheter for 2 years. He is well, eating and drinking normally, with no fever, confusion or suprapubic pain. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg. A routine catheter urine sample grows E. coli.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common with catheters (biofilm) and should not be treated. If a symptomatic UTI develops, change the catheter.

steps.x: Management of a culture result in a catheterised patient.

clues: no fever, confusion or suprapubic pain
steps.x: Catheterised with bacteria but no symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Do not treat** asymptomatic bacteriuria.

elim: Not indicated for bacteriuria.
He is well; no infection to treat.
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria drives resistance.
Same: no symptoms, no treatment.

steps.x: **B. Do not treat with antibiotics.** Catheter + bacteriuria + no symptoms = no antibiotics.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman who is 26 weeks pregnant develops acute pyelonephritis 3 days after untreated dysuria. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely reason pregnancy predisposes to this complication?
practice.e: Progesterone causes ureteric dilation and reduced peristalsis, allowing ascending infection. This is why even asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy.

steps.x: Science: explain why pregnancy leads to pyelonephritis.
Infection climbed from bladder to kidney during pregnancy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Progesterone** dilates ureters and reduces peristalsis: urine stasis lets infection ascend.

elim: Not stated, and not the main mechanism.
Normal in pregnancy; it does not drive ascent.
Urethral length does not change.
Not the key mechanism.

steps.x: **D. Progesterone-mediated ureteric dilation.** Pregnancy pyelonephritis = progesterone ureteric dilation.
